abstract: This Deloitte survey of over 11,000 workers across 17 countries examines how organizations can leverage AI and human collaboration to address workforce challenges created by demographic shifts and labor shortages. The research identifies four key opportunities: enabling human-machine teaming, implementing agentic AI while keeping humans on the loop, using AI for skill development, and accelerating knowledge transfer. The findings reveal that most workers prefer a mix of human and AI collaboration, though they perceive AI as faster and humans as delivering higher quality work, particularly for tasks requiring complex judgment and empathy.
keyFindings: By 2030, 1 in 6 people globally will be over age 60, while the number of US high school graduates is expected to peak in 2025 and then decline throughout the next decade, creating significant labor shortages and skills gaps.

Most workers across all age groups prefer an even mix of human and AI collaboration, with only younger workers (18-44) showing stronger preference for AI-only tools and older workers preferring human-only collaboration.

Across multiple tasks including problem solving, creativity, and training, workers ages 18-44 report that AI helps them deliver faster results, though respondents across all age groups rate human colleagues higher on quality and feedback.

Sixty-one percent of survey respondents believe AI can support upskilling opportunities for entry-level workers, with workers ages 25-34 most likely to agree (66%), and 60% agree AI can help experienced workers share knowledge across the organization.

By 2027, Deloitte anticipates that 50% of firms currently using generative AI will at least be piloting agentic AI, which could increase worker productivity but also raises questions about optimizing human and machine team structures.
methodology: Deloitte surveyed 11,387 full-time (81%) and part-time workers (19%) between February 20 and February 27, 2025, spread across 17 countries including the EMEA region (45%), the APAC region (32%), and the Americas (24%). Respondents represented a mix of ages, experience levels, industries, and business functions and were asked about their use of and attitudes toward AI, work motivations, interest in alternative work models, and retirement plans. Logistic regression was used to generate predictive probabilities based on workers' ratings.
qualifiers: The survey was conducted in February 2025, limiting longer-term predictive validity. While the sample spans 17 countries and multiple regions, some findings may not be generalizable across all global markets. The research acknowledges that worker preferences for AI versus human collaboration will likely evolve alongside technological capabilities. Authors note that the youngest workers entering the workforce as 'AI-natives' may have different preferences than those surveyed. Several key findings rely on self-reported worker perceptions rather than objective performance metrics. Some role-based findings show high variation (e.g., sales and trade workers show notably lower agreement on AI's role in knowledge transfer compared to executives and office workers), suggesting context-specific limitations.
